strengths: WildFeedback addresses an important NLP problem: learning from feedback that users naturally provide during conversations. The 20,281-example dataset, accompanying preference summaries, and model-specific variants constitute a potentially useful resource beyond the proposed training pipeline.

The experiments provide credible evidence of training utility across three model families and three established benchmarks. For example, Phi-3 trained on WF GPT-4 improves from 24.3 to 34.9 on AlpacaEval’s length-controlled win rate and from 15.4 to 32.4 on Arena-Hard. These external benchmark results strengthen the evidence beyond the proposed checklist evaluation.

The paper includes meaningful validation and documentation: human annotation studies with human-human agreement baselines, regenerated UltraFeedback comparisons, reported separation of training and test users and conversations, detailed prompts, and major training hyperparameters. The pipeline is understandable, and the limitations acknowledge noisy feedback and selection bias.
weaknesses: The central claim of more faithful alignment with real users needs stronger independent validation. GPT-4 extracts preference summaries, generates or filters training pairs, and judges the resulting responses. Figure 2 establishes that checklists influence judgments, but does not establish that those judgments better recover users’ preferences. Appendix C reports 57.14% agreement with humans (κ=0.372), against 63.27% human-human agreement, without comparing checklist and checklist-free accuracy against independently verified preferences. Auditing summary faithfulness and pair labels against the original feedback would address the main concern preventing a clear Findings recommendation.

The experiments do not isolate the contribution of authentic feedback. WildFeedback and UltraFeedback differ in prompt source, conversational context, response construction, and filtering. Consequently, their comparison cannot determine how much improvement comes from feedback conditioning versus other dataset differences. A controlled experiment on the same WildChat prompts using genuine feedback, omitted feedback, and generic revision instructions would substantially strengthen the methodological claim.

The 540-example evaluation set deliberately selects central preferences within clusters and tasks resembling training tasks. This supports evaluation on that curated population, but does not establish representativeness of the majority of users. Feedback selection and the detector’s 48.4% DSAT recall further restrict coverage. Claims about diverse, evolving user preferences and reduced bias exceed the demonstrated scope.

Claims of consistent, significant superiority over UltraFeedback are overstated. In Table 3, Qwen-2 WF GPT-4 underperforms UF GPT-4 on AlpacaEval LC (39.4 versus 40.6) and MT-Bench (7.60 versus 7.66); several other improvements are small. Confidence intervals or repeated-run variability are absent, limiting confidence in the comparative advantages despite the clearer gains over the original models.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful appendices. The manuscript does not sufficiently specify the embeddings and clustering procedure, exact split and user-grouping construction, generation settings, or hyperparameter-selection protocol. It should also explicitly state whether extracted preference summaries are supplied to the trained models during training and inference, beyond their documented use in response synthesis and judging.
